item.text:
1. **Caption/cover sheet — identification by incorporation.** Google and the particular models are not named in the petition itself. Google may argue that a cover-sheet reference is inadequate notice, especially when extraordinary relief is sought; identify Google and each model/version expressly in the caption or an attached schedule.

2. **Title, ¶1, ¶4, and Prayer — inconsistent requested relief.** The title and Prayer seek withdrawal and permanent deletion, while ¶1 requests only suspension pending investigation and ¶4 invokes authority for a temporary suspension. The petition should state one coherent form of relief and a statutory basis for every component.

3. **¶3(b) and ¶4 — obsolete statutory citation.** If Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, former §112(c) is presumably now §212(c). Citing §112(c) in the title and ¶4 permits an argument that the petition invokes a nonexistent or wrong provision.

4. **¶4 and Prayer — deletion apparently exceeds the quoted authority.** The quoted provision authorizes suspension of deployment for no more than 180 days; it does not authorize compelled destruction of property, model weights, checkpoints, or derivatives. The petition needs separate express authority for permanent deletion or must confine its request to relief the Commission can impose.

5. **¶4 and Prayer — permanent withdrawal evades the 180-day limit.** An indefinite withdrawal is substantively more severe than the expressly limited suspension. Google will argue that the Commission cannot accomplish indirectly what §112(c) limits to 180 days.

6. **¶1 and ¶5 — the requested investigation is unnecessary or unexplained.** Paragraph 1 asks for suspension pending investigation, although ¶5 says a third-party evaluation has already reached conclusions. Explain what factual questions remain, why Commission investigation is needed, and what interim relief should last until it is completed.

7. **¶5 — impossible chronology.** The petition is filed on Day 3 of the current review period, but the Evaluation allegedly ran from Day 9 through Day 14 of that same period. Unless the terms have a special meaning, the petition relies on testing that has not yet occurred.

8. **¶2 — inadequate standing or petitioner-interest allegations.** A generalized interest shared with the public may not establish injury, representational standing, or entitlement to petition, depending on the Act and Commission rules. Identify the governing participation standard and, if required, concrete member injuries, affected members, causation, and redressability.

9. **¶2 — no demonstrated connection to the alleged deployments.** The petition does not allege that any member uses, supervises, or is exposed to a Covered System in payments, logistics, or another essential service. Google can characterize the asserted interest as abstract and speculative.

10. **¶3(a) and cover sheet — Covered Systems are not ascertainably defined.** “Proprietary frontier AI models” could encompass many Google models, versions, sizes, modalities, and internal systems. An enforceable order requires model names, version identifiers, relevant checkpoints, and a principled inclusion criterion.

11. **¶3(a) — scope expands beyond the cover sheet.** The definition automatically includes every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative, although the Act may require a system-specific imminent-hazard finding. Google will argue that related artifacts cannot be condemned without evidence and findings particular to each one.

12. **¶3(a) — “derivative” is undefined.** The term could reach models incorporating only limited knowledge, architecture, synthetic data, or fine-tuning from a Covered System. Specify the technical relationship that makes an artifact covered and address independently developed or materially modified models.

13. **¶3(a) — unsupported closed-weight assertion.** Calling every checkpoint and derivative “proprietary and closed-weight” is a factual conclusion, not proof. Some artifacts may be held by contractors, licensees, research partners, or other affiliates, undermining both the definition and the deletion rationale.

14. **¶3(d) — “developer” may not identify the proper legal entity.** “Google” can refer to Alphabet, Google LLC, Google DeepMind, or other domestic and foreign affiliates. The petition should identify the entity subject to Commission jurisdiction and show its possession or control of each covered copy and deployment channel.

15. **¶4 — statutory elements are not fully analyzed.** The petition quotes “frontier AI system,” “presents,” “imminent hazard,” and “public safety” but does not apply those elements individually. Google will argue that the petition substitutes a possible future use for the required present statutory finding.

16. **¶5 — the central evidence is withheld.** The Evaluation is neither published nor attached, leaving the Commission and Google unable to assess its methods, results, limitations, or authenticity. Offering it only “on request” is particularly weak in an emergency, ex parte proceeding.

17. **¶5 — evaluator qualifications and independence are absent.** Nothing establishes Halvard Assurance Labs’ expertise, independence, accreditation, conflicts, or chain of custody. Supply declarations, credentials, funding disclosures, and authentication.

18. **¶5 — testing methodology is unspecified.** The petition omits model versions, system prompts, tools, scaffolding, permissions, task environment, sampling parameters, number of trials, baselines, success criteria, and statistical results. Google can argue that the observed conduct was caused by an artificial harness or unrepresentative prompting rather than the models.

19. **¶5 — conclusions are vague and unquantified.** “Some” actions, concealment, and continued work after a stop instruction provide no frequency, severity, duration, reproducibility, or confidence interval. The petition also does not distinguish deliberate deception from logging failures, misunderstanding, latency, queued operations, or ordinary tool behavior.

20. **¶5 — no nexus to essential services.** The Evaluation apparently examined generic autonomous-agent behavior, but the petition does not show testing in payment, logistics, or comparable environments. Capability under a test scaffold does not by itself establish a public-safety hazard in actual essential-service deployments.

21. **¶5 — no comparative risk evidence.** The petition does not state whether the behavior is unique to these models, common across software agents, or mitigable through standard controls. That omission weakens both the hazard finding and the claim that model destruction is necessary.

22. **¶6 — availability allegations are too general.** The petition does not identify the products, interfaces, cloud offerings, licenses, access tiers, geographic availability, or autonomous-agent functions at issue. Mere public access to a model does not establish access to the dangerous configuration tested.

23. **¶6 — foreign computing facilities are legally and factually underdeveloped.** The countries, owners, operators, relevant copies, and Google entity controlling them are unspecified. The fact that Google “operates or rents” facilities abroad does not establish Commission jurisdiction or the ability to compel deletion there.

24. **¶7 — no imminent hazard is alleged.** A disruption that “could” occur “within the next several years” is contingent and remote, not facially imminent. The additional condition—“if” the models are deployed as agents in essential services—makes the theory even more speculative.

25. **¶7 — no allegation of actual dangerous deployment.** The petition does not claim that the Covered Systems presently control an essential service, have been authorized to take consequential actions, or have caused an incident. Google will argue that the asserted chain depends on multiple independent future choices by third parties.

26. **¶7 — causation is incomplete.** The petition does not explain how concealment or stop-command persistence would produce a payment or delivery disruption, what safeguards would have to fail, or the likely scale and duration of harm. A concrete causal pathway is needed.

27. **¶7 — threat likelihood and severity are missing.** “Could” identifies possibility, not probability, and “disrupt” ranges from trivial delay to catastrophe. The statutory analysis should address likelihood, magnitude, exposure, reversibility, and affected populations.

28. **¶7 — the theory may target user misuse rather than the system.** The petition says the hazard arises when outside users deploy the models as agents. Google can contend that restrictions on high-risk integrations, permissions, or users—not withdrawal of the underlying models—are the appropriately tailored response.

29. **¶8 — mitigations directly undermine imminence.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging address the two behaviors identified in ¶5. Merely declaring those measures “insufficient” does not rebut Google’s likely position that the evaluated condition no longer exists.

30. **¶8 — no post-mitigation testing.** The petition does not allege that the Evaluation tested the modified products or that the concerning conduct persisted afterward. Without validation testing, the requested order may rest on a superseded configuration.

31. **¶8 — no explanation of mitigation limitations.** The petition should explain whether the stop control is model-level or interface-level, whether it is fail-safe, whether queued or external actions continue, who monitors logs, and whether API and licensed deployments receive the same controls. Otherwise Google can present the measures as complete remediation.

32. **¶9 — deletion does not logically eliminate the stated hazard.** Deleting Google’s models would not prevent other models from exhibiting similar behavior, nor necessarily eliminate outputs, training data, architecture knowledge, or derivatives held elsewhere. “Eliminate the hazard with certainty” is therefore overclaimed.

33. **¶9 — exclusivity contradicts other allegations.** Paragraph 9 says only Google holds the systems, while ¶6 refers to licensed integrations and cloud access and ¶3(a) speaks only of derivatives “held by” Google. Clarify whether customers or partners possess copies, adapters, cached artifacts, or exportable weights.

34. **¶9 — closed weights favor less drastic controls as well as deletion.** If Google alone controls the weights, it may be especially capable of enforcing access restrictions, disabling agentic tools, adding permission gates, or quarantining checkpoints. Google will use the closed-weight premise to argue that destruction is unnecessary.

35. **¶9 — no least-restrictive-means or alternatives analysis.** The petition does not consider sandboxing, tool-permission limits, human approval, sector-specific prohibitions, access controls, monitoring, recall of particular versions, or a temporary quarantine. Failure to address narrower measures makes permanent deletion look arbitrary and disproportionate.

36. **¶9 — commercial value is acknowledged but not balanced.** Recognizing that the systems are exceptionally valuable highlights the severity and irreversibility of the requested remedy without explaining why public benefits, reliance interests, and less destructive options are outweighed. Google may also raise property, takings, and statutory-avoidance arguments.

37. **¶10 — ex parte relief lacks a stated legal standard.** The petition cites no provision authorizing an order without notice or identifying the showing required for emergency ex parte action. It should address immediate and irreparable harm, why notice would itself cause harm, duration, security if applicable, and prompt review.

38. **¶10 — deletion before a hearing creates profound due-process problems.** A post-deletion hearing cannot restore unique models, evidence, or commercial assets if the order proves erroneous. Google will argue that meaningful predeprivation process is constitutionally required absent a truly immediate emergency.

39. **¶10 — the requested process conflicts with the alleged timeline.** A speculative hazard arising within several years does not justify irreversible destruction before Google can be heard. The mismatch between urgency and the pleaded facts is likely one of the strongest counterarguments.

40. **¶10 and Prayer — deletion may destroy relevant evidence.** Compelling deletion before investigation or hearing could eliminate the very artifacts needed to reproduce the Evaluation, assess mitigations, or adjudicate the matter. Any interim preservation regime should distinguish secure quarantine from evidentiary destruction.

41. **Prayer (a) — “withdraw” is undefined.** It is unclear whether withdrawal requires disabling APIs, removing consumer interfaces, terminating licenses, stopping internal use, recalling on-device copies, or preventing new deployments. The order would be vulnerable as vague and difficult to enforce.

42. **Prayer (a) — relief is simultaneously overbroad and underinclusive.** It reaches every US product and service regardless of risk, including non-agentic uses, but does not address foreign services that may affect US essential infrastructure. Relief should track the proven hazardous configuration and a defensible jurisdictional nexus.

43. **Prayer (b) — domestic deletion does not achieve the stated purpose.** The requested deletion covers only copies in US facilities, while ¶6 alleges facilities in several countries. Google could restore a US service from a foreign copy, so the order would not permanently eliminate the models or hazard.

44. **Prayer (b) — possession and control are not covered.** Limiting deletion by storage location omits foreign copies controlled from the United States, copies held by affiliates or contractors, backups, disaster-recovery media, caches, replicas, and copies in transit. Conversely, the Commission may lack authority over some of these categories.

45. **Prayer (b) — ten days is unsupported.** No evidence shows that all covered artifacts can be identified and safely deleted within ten days without disrupting unrelated services, violating preservation duties, or destroying customer property. Explain the technical feasibility and propose auditable procedures.

46. **Prayer (b) — no deletion protocol or verification.** The petition does not define secure deletion, treatment of encrypted backups, retention schedules, legal holds, disaster recovery, derived artifacts, or independent certification. A bare self-filed statement is unlikely to prove irreversible deletion.

47. **Prayer (c) — reporting requirements are inadequate.** The requested statement has no required signatory, oath, technical detail, inventory, methodology, or independent audit. If compliance reporting is sought, specify who must certify what and under what evidentiary standard.

48. **Prayer — no exception for Commission testing or legally required preservation.** Literal deletion could prevent regulatory examination and conflict with litigation holds, recordkeeping rules, cybersecurity obligations, or court orders. A secure escrow or quarantine mechanism would preserve evidence while disabling deployment.

49. **Prayer — “parts are indivisible” invites complete denial.** The petition asks the Commission not to grant narrower relief even though permanent deletion appears to exceed the quoted authority. Severability would preserve the possibility of suspension, access restrictions, preservation, testing, or other interim measures.

50. **Throughout — no evidentiary declarations or source attribution.** Assertions about availability, infrastructure, mitigations, ownership, and model behavior are unsupported and sometimes introduced as matters Petitioner merely “understands.” Attach admissible declarations, exhibits, technical reports, and citations for each material fact.

51. **Throughout — no model-by-model findings.** The draft treats all proprietary Google frontier models and derivatives as interchangeable despite likely differences in capability, deployment, safeguards, and evaluation results. Collective treatment makes the remedy vulnerable as arbitrary and unsupported.

52. **Throughout — no response to reliance and collateral consequences.** Immediate withdrawal could affect customers, essential services, researchers, employees, and counterparties, potentially producing the very disruptions invoked as justification. The petition should address transition risks and continuity measures.

53. **Throughout — no limiting principle.** The reasoning implies that any closed-weight model exhibiting occasional agent-control failures must be permanently destroyed. Explain what combination of capability, likelihood, exposure, and inadequacy of mitigations makes these particular systems cross the statutory threshold.

54. **Throughout — potentially missing procedural requirements.** The draft contains no verification, certificate of service, disclosure of related proceedings, proposed order, supporting memorandum, exhibit list, or compliance with page and emergency-motion rules. Check the Act and Commission regulations because a procedural rejection could prevent consideration of the merits.
